date.note: Completed by Moses ben Jacob Cordovero (the Ramak) in Safed in 1548, when its author was in his mid-twenties; first printed at Kraków (Cracow) in 1591. The digitized Hebrew and English text on Sefaria is under the Kabbalah category (Ramak); the English is the Sefaria Community Translation (CC0).

summary: The Pardes Rimonim ('Orchard of Pomegranates'), completed by Moses Cordovero (the Ramak) in Safed in 1548, is a systematic summa of the theoretical kabbalah that had developed since the Zohar, organized into thirty-two 'gates' (she'arim) subdivided into chapters, which gathers, harmonizes, and analyzes the received doctrines of the sefirot, the divine names, and the emanated worlds. Treated in the tradition and in scholarship as the first comprehensive and orderly synthesis of pre-Lurianic kabbalah, it became a standard reference for the study of theoretical kabbalah in the generation before Isaac Luria's system reframed the field.
description:
The Pardes Rimonim ('Orchard of Pomegranates') is the major theoretical work of Moses ben Jacob Cordovero (1522-1570), known by the acronym the Ramak, completed in Safed (Tzfat) in 1548 and first printed at Kraków in 1591. It sets out to gather the kabbalah that had accumulated since the Zohar into a single ordered system, and the tradition and modern scholarship alike treat it as the first comprehensive and orderly synthesis of that material. The account that follows presents the work's teaching as the work's own attributed exposition rather than as claims the editor affirms or denies.

The book is arranged as a set of 'gates' (she'arim), thirty-two of them, each subdivided into chapters, so that the whole reads as a topic-by-topic reference on the doctrines of theoretical kabbalah: the nature and number of the sefirot, their relation to the Infinite (Ein Sof), the divine names, the letters of the alphabet, the structure of the emanated worlds, and related themes. The work opens (Gate I, in the open Sefaria text) with the gate 'called "Ten and not nine"', which takes up the foundational teaching that the sefirot are ten: 'It is well-known and eminent that all those who engage in this hidden wisdom unanimously consent that the number of the Sefirot is ten, and there is no disagreement at all in this matter.' Cordovero grounds this in the Sefer Yetzirah ('Book of Formation'), which he cites, 'Ten Sefirot without what(-ness) [beli-mah], the number of ten fingers, five opposite five, and the single covenant standing in the middle', and glosses beli-mah as beli mah, 'without quiddity / essence', so that the sefirot are said to be ten in number yet 'without an essence that is comprehensible to human beings, because they are not limited and grasped'. The first gate then works through the difficulties in that verse in order, in the manner of the whole book, a received datum stated, the problems in it enumerated, and a harmonizing exposition given.

Cordovero's synthesis is generally described in scholarship as the high point of the theosophical, theoretical kabbalah that preceded Isaac Luria (the Arizal). A recurring problem the Pardes addresses is the relation between the transcendent Infinite (Ein Sof) and the sefirot through which, on the kabbalists' account, the divine acts and is known: whether the sefirot are the divine essence itself or vessels or instruments of it, a question the work treats at length and for which it became a standard point of reference. Luria arrived in Safed near the end of Cordovero's life, and the new system he taught, with its distinctive doctrines of the contraction (tzimtzum), the shattering of the vessels (shevirat ha-kelim), and cosmic repair (tikkun), reframed and in the later reception in large part superseded Cordovero's synthesis; later kabbalists and Hasidic authors nonetheless continued to study the two together, citing Cordovero's Pardes and 'the Kabbalah of the Arizal' side by side (Shneur Zalman of Liady's Tanya does so explicitly). This entry states the relation between the two systems as the tradition and scholarship describe it, without ranking their truth.

This entry presents the Pardes Rimonim on Judaism's own terms as Cordovero's systematic reference work for theoretical kabbalah, with its doctrines of the sefirot, the divine names, and the emanated worlds attributed to the work and its author and described, not adjudicated, by the editor. The kabbalah whose doctrines it systematizes is reported as the tradition's own subject matter, not affirmed as metaphysics.

NEUTRALITY (neutrality #1, #4, #6): the doctrines the work systematizes, the ten sefirot, their relation to Ein Sof, the divine names, and the emanated worlds, are stated throughout as the WORK'S OWN ATTRIBUTED exposition ('presents the work's teaching as the work's own attributed exposition', 'attributed to the work and its author and described, not adjudicated'); the kabbalah it gathers is DESCRIBED as the tradition's subject matter, not affirmed as metaphysics by the editor. SOURCING triangulates three lenses per neutrality #8-#9: (b) the PRIMARY text itself, open and auditable on Sefaria (Sefaria Community Translation, English CC0; Hebrew public domain), Gate I chapter 1 ('Ten and not nine') READ LINE-BY-LINE; (a) academic monographs on Cordovero, Joseph (Yosef) Ben-Shlomo, Torat ha-Elohut shel R. Moshe Cordovero ('The Mystical Theology of Moses Cordovero'; Jerusalem: Bialik Institute, 1965), the standard scholarly study of Cordovero's speculative system, and Bracha Sack, Be-Sha'arei ha-Kabbalah shel Rabbi Moshe Cordovero (Ben-Gurion University Press, 1995), the standard modern Cordovero scholar; and (c) a contemporary Jewish scholar on-topic, Moshe Idel, Kabbalah: New Perspectives (Yale, 1988), on the theoretical kabbalah of the period and the sefirot / Ein Sof problem the Pardes addresses. No encyclopedias (no Encyclopaedia Judaica, no Encyclopedia.com, no Chabad.org, no My Jewish Learning), no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. CONFIDENCE / HONESTY: the Pardes Rimonim IS openly available on Sefaria with an English translation (Sefaria Community Translation, CC0), and Gate I chapter 1 was READ LINE-BY-LINE via the Sefaria text API on 2026-07-26 and its load-bearing lines confirmed verbatim: the gate 'called "Ten and not nine"'; 'the number of the Sefirot is ten, and there is no disagreement at all in this matter'; the citation of Sefer Yetzirah 1:3, 'Ten Sefirot without what(-ness), the number of ten fingers, five opposite five, and the single covenant standing in the middle'; and the gloss of beli-mah as 'without quiddity/essence', the sefirot being 'without an essence that is comprehensible to human beings'. The primary is therefore rated HIGH. The 1548 completion date, the first printing at Kraków 1591, and the thirty-two-gate (she'arim) structure are confirmed across the scholarship; the text itself references its later gates by number (e.g. 'the Gate of the Soul [XXXI]', 'the Gate of Atsilut, Beriah, Yetsirah, Asiya [Gate XVI]'), consistent with the thirty-two-gate structure. The three monographs (Ben-Shlomo, Sack, Idel) are MEDIUM, verified to exist and be on-topic via publisher / library records, not read line-by-line; Sack carries the same medium rating she holds in cordovero.json. sources.citation: Moses Cordovero. Pardes Rimonim ('Orchard of Pomegranates'), Gate I ('the First Gate which is called "Ten and not nine"'), chapter 1; completed Safed 1548, first printed Kraków 1591. Open Hebrew and English text on Sefaria (Kabbalah / Ramak). Cited as the openly-auditable primary text carrying the work's load-bearing systematic exposition, read line-by-line and verified verbatim: the gate opens 'It is well-known and eminent that all those who engage in this hidden wisdom unanimously consent that the number of the Sefirot is ten, and there is no disagreement at all in this matter'; it cites Sefer Yetzirah 1:3, 'Ten Sefirot without what(-ness), the number of ten fingers, five opposite five, and the single covenant standing in the middle'; and it glosses beli-mah as beli mah, 'without quiddity/essence', the sefirot being 'without an essence that is comprehensible to human beings, because they are not limited and grasped'. The text references its later gates by number (the Gate of the Soul [XXXI], the Gate of Atsilut-Beriah-Yetsirah-Asiya [XVI]), consistent with the thirty-two-gate (she'arim) structure. Read line-by-line via the Sefaria text API (2026-07-26).

sources.citation: Ben-Shlomo, Joseph (Yosef). Torat ha-Elohut shel R. Moshe Cordovero ('The Mystical Theology of Moses Cordovero'). Jerusalem: Bialik Institute (Mosad Bialik), 1965 (in Hebrew; 336 pp.). The standard full-length scholarly study of Cordovero's speculative system as set out in the Pardes Rimonim and his other works, treating the doctrine of the sefirot and the relation of Ein Sof to the sefirot; originally a doctoral dissertation. Cited as the principal academic lens on the Pardes specifically. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Bialik Institute catalogue record; the author was a scholar of Cordovero), not read line-by-line.
sources.license: Proprietary; cited for reference (a 1967 scholarly review of the book in the Revue des etudes juives, on Persee, confirms the work exists and its subject).

sources.citation: Sack, Bracha. Be-Sha'arei ha-Kabbalah shel Rabbi Moshe Cordovero ('In the Gates of the Kabbalah of Rabbi Moses Cordovero'). Be'er Sheva: Ben-Gurion University of the Negev Press, 1995. The standard modern scholarly monograph on Cordovero's kabbalah, analyzing the doctrine of the sefirot and the divine emanation as systematized in the Pardes Rimonim and Cordovero's other works. Cited as a second academic lens on the Pardes. Verified to exist and be on-topic (the author is the standard Cordovero scholar at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev), not read line-by-line; carries the same medium rating it holds in cordovero.json.

sources.citation: Idel, Moshe. Kabbalah: New Perspectives. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1988 (xx + 419 pp.; ISBN 9780300046991). A study by a contemporary Jewish scholar (Hebrew University) of the phenomenology and history of the kabbalah, treating the theoretical kabbalah of the sixteenth century, the sefirot, and the relation of the Infinite (Ein Sof) to the sefirot that the Pardes Rimonim systematizes; cited as the contemporary-Jewish-scholar lens on the theoretical kabbalah the work gathers. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Yale University Press record; AJS Review notice), not read line-by-line.
